content: 1. Greywater refers to the total volume of water generated from household activities, excluding water from toilets. 2. A hazard is any biological, chemical, or physical constituent that has the potential to cause harm to human health. 3. A hazardous event is any incident or situation that introduces or releases a hazard into the environment where humans live or work, amplifies the concentration of a hazard in such an environment, or fails to remove a hazard from the human environment. 4. Legislation refers to the collective body of laws and the process of creating or enacting these laws. 5. The term local community in this context refers to individuals who live or work near or downstream from a sanitation system and may be affected by it, either actively or passively. 6. A low-income country is defined as one with a Gross National Income (GNI) per capita of $995 or less, as calculated using the World Bank Atlas method in 2017. 7. Manual emptying refers to the process of removing faecal sludge from on-site sanitation technologies, where human labor is required to physically lift the sludge. This process can involve either manual or motorized transport. 8. Manual transport refers to the human-powered transportation of faecal sludge emptied from on-site sanitation technologies. It can be used in conjunction with either manual or motorized emptying methods. 9. Middle-income countries are classified into two categories: lower middle-income economies, with a GNI per capita between $996 and $3,895, and upper middle-income economies, with a GNI per capita between $3,896 and $12,055, as calculated using the World Bank Atlas method. 10. Motorized emptying involves the use of motorized equipment to remove faecal sludge from on-site sanitation technologies. While humans operate the equipment and maneuver the hose, the sludge is not manually lifted. This method is often followed by motorized transport but can also be used with manual transport. 11. Motorized transport refers to the use of motorized equipment for transporting faecal sludge from on-site sanitation technologies. Humans operate the equipment, but the sludge is not manually transported. This method can be used with either motorized or manual emptying. 12. Nutrient management is a treatment objective focused on managing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium through specific treatment technologies. 13. Off-site sanitation refers to a sanitation system where excreta (wastewater) is collected and transported away from the location where it is generated, typically relying on sewer technology for transport. 14. On-site sanitation refers to a sanitation system where excreta (faecal sludge) is collected, stored, and either emptied or treated on the same plot of land where it is generated. 15. An open drain is an open channel designed to carry greywater, surface water, or stormwater. 16. An outlet is a pipe or hole through which wastewater is discharged or gases are vented. 17. Overflow refers to an outlet designed to discharge excess wastewater. 18. A plan is a detailed and time-bound proposal aimed at achieving specific objectives. 19. Policy refers to a course or principle of action adopted or proposed by an organization or individual, such as a government, political party, or business, to influence and determine decisions, actions, and other matters. 20. A public toilet is a facility not restricted to specific users and may be formally or informally managed. 21. Regulation refers to the act or process of controlling or being controlled. Regulations are rules or directives established and maintained by an authority. 22. Risk is the likelihood and potential consequences of an event with a negative impact occurring. 23. A sanitary inspection is an on-site evaluation conducted by qualified individuals to assess all conditions, devices, and practices within a sanitation system that may pose actual or potential risks to the health and well-being of exposed groups. This process identifies system deficiencies, including potential sources of hazardous events and inadequacies in system integrity. 24. The sanitation service chain encompasses all components and processes of a sanitation system, from toilet capture and containment to emptying, transport, treatment (on-site or off-site), and final disposal or end use. 25. A sanitation system is a context-specific series of sanitation technologies and services designed to manage faecal sludge and/or wastewater through the stages of containment, emptying, transport, treatment, and end use or disposal. 26. Sanitation technologies refer to the specific infrastructure, methods, or services designed to manage faecal sludge and/or wastewater through the stages of containment, emptying, transport, treatment, and end use or disposal. 27. Sanitation users are all individuals who use a toilet. 28. Sanitation workers are individuals, whether employed or not, responsible for cleaning, maintaining, operating, or emptying sanitation technologies at any stage of the sanitation chain. 29. A separate (foul) sewer is a sewer system that carries blackwater and greywater but excludes stormwater. 30. Sewage refers to wastewater transported through a sewer system. 31. A sewer is an underground pipe system that transports blackwater, greywater, and, in some cases, stormwater (in combined sewers) from households and other users to treatment plants, using gravity or pumps as needed. 32. A shared toilet is a single toilet facility used by two or more households. 33. A soak pit is a pit or chamber that allows effluent to infiltrate into the surrounding ground. 34. Stabilization is a process achieved through the biodegradation of readily degradable molecules, resulting in faecal sludge with a lower oxygen demand. This treatment objective produces faecal sludge containing more stable, complex organic molecules that are not easily degradable. 35. A standard is a required or agreed level of quality or attainment. 36. Stormwater refers to rainfall runoff collected from roofs, roads, and other surfaces before flowing toward low-lying areas. It is the portion of rainfall that does not infiltrate into the soil. 37. A theory of change is a comprehensive description and illustration of how and why a desired change is expected to occur in a specific context. 38. A toilet is the user interface with the sanitation system, where excreta is captured. It can include various types of toilet seats, latrine slabs, pedestals, pans, or urinals. Examples include pour-flush toilets, cistern-flush toilets, dry toilets, and urine-diverting toilets. 39. Treatment refers to processes that alter the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics or composition of faecal sludge or wastewater, converting it into a product that is safe for end use or disposal. 40. Urine is the liquid produced by the body to excrete urea and other waste products. In this context, urine refers to pure urine that is not mixed with faeces or water. 41. Wastewater is used water originating from a combination of domestic (households and services), industrial, and stormwater sources, as well as any sewer inflow or infiltration. 42. WHO guidelines are documents containing recommendations on health interventions, including clinical, public health, or policy-related recommendations. 43. The WHO Guidelines on Sanitation and Health emphasize the importance of safe sanitation for health, from preventing infections to improving mental and social well-being. These guidelines, developed in accordance with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, provide comprehensive advice on maximizing the health impact of sanitation interventions. They summarize evidence on the links between sanitation and health, offer evidence-informed recommendations, and provide guidance for international, national, and local sanitation policies and programs. The guidelines also highlight the role of health authorities in sanitation policy and programming to ensure health risks are effectively identified and managed. The intended audience includes national and local authorities responsible for the safety of sanitation systems and services, such as policymakers, planners, and implementers within and outside the health sector, as well as those involved in developing, implementing, and monitoring sanitation standards and regulations.
